_comment: MCP sandbox seccomp profile. Starts from Docker's upstream default (deny-by-default with a large allow list) and adds explicit deny actions for syscalls that Node 20 + Vite + npm install have no business calling. Wire via `--security-opt seccomp=<this-file>` (CliOciDriver does this when isolation.seccompProfile is set). Tested on Linux kernel 5.15+; older kernels will still load it but some denied syscalls may be unknown and get silently dropped — that's fine because the goal is defense-in-depth, not a precise whitelist.

syscalls._comment: Filesystem-layer mounts — the sandbox has no legitimate reason to mount anything. Blocks container escape via bind-mount tricks.
Namespace manipulation — creating new namespaces from inside the container is a classic escalation vector (user namespaces give effective root inside the new ns).
Kernel module / kexec — never needed from userspace apps, always a privilege escalation or boot-integrity attack surface.
Reboot / power-state control. No, the LLM does not get to reboot the host.
eBPF + perf — powerful kernel introspection / patching. Vite doesn't need them; blocking them removes a large kernel-surface attack vector.
ptrace — used by debuggers and by escape exploits to hijack neighbour processes. npm install doesn't use it; `node --inspect` uses a TCP port, not ptrace.
Legacy system call suite — rarely used by modern glibc/musl, occasionally used by rootkits.
Time-of-day tampering — a guest that can set clock forward breaks HMAC expiry checks and could desync logs.
Quota / device-node controls — need CAP_SYS_ADMIN which we already dropped, but belt + suspenders.
I/O port access — x86-only, used to talk directly to hardware. Nothing in Node touches this.
Obscure process-personality flags (swapping personalities can bypass ASLR / hide exploits).
